title: Everyday Economics
description: Ten calm stories and columns about how money works in everyday life: food prices, a farmers' co-op, a bed and breakfast, a paid-off loan, neighborhood money, online selling, a market stand, a repair club, choosing a profession and a small cinema.

lessons.title: Why Food Costs What It Costs
lessons.summary: A price analyst explains, in a calm newspaper column, where the money for our food really goes.
lessons.text:
Why Food Costs What It Costs
By Helen Moore

Almost every week, a reader writes to ask me the same question: why is food so expensive? I have worked as a price analyst for 20 years. As an analyst, I follow the prices of bread, milk and vegetables from the farm all the way to your local store.

The first myth is that farmers become rich whenever prices rise. In fact, the farmer usually receives only a small part of what you pay. When you buy bread for 4 dollars, the grain inside it may be worth less than 30 cents. The rest pays for transport, packaging, workers, rent, electricity and the store's profit. The rich farmer, I am afraid, is only a myth.

The second myth is that big stores raise prices simply because they can. It is true that in many towns one or two chains are dominant, and a dominant chain has great power over the companies that sell to it. However, food stores usually keep only 2 or 3 cents of profit on every dollar. Their incentive is to sell a lot, not to charge a lot. A store that consistently charges more than the store across the road soon loses its customers.

Many stores now sell their own products in three tiers. The lowest tier is cheap and plain, the middle tier carries a familiar brand, and the top tier comes in fine boxes with gold letters. The milk in the lowest tier is often the same milk as in the middle tier. Furthermore, the top tier is not always better; sometimes it is just better dressed.

Regulatory costs, such as safety tests and clear labels, add a little to every product. I believe these regulatory costs are worth paying, because they protect us all.

Then there is excess. Every year, stores throw away food that nobody bought, and the cost of this excess is hidden in the price of everything else. Furthermore, when we buy more than we can eat, we pay for our own excess twice.

Readers sometimes ask me about the accuracy of the price numbers in the news. Their accuracy is generally good, but an average can hide a great deal. If the price of coffee doubles while rice gets cheaper, the average may hardly move, even though your own bill has grown. Prices that rise consistently for many months matter more than one bad week.

My advice is simple. Compare the tiers, buy what you will really eat, and do not believe every myth you hear.

Questions:
What does Helen do as an analyst?
She follows the prices of food from the farm all the way to the store.
Why do food stores have an incentive to sell a lot?
They keep only 2 or 3 cents of profit on every dollar, so they need to sell a lot.
Is the top tier always better?
No, it is not; sometimes it is just better dressed.
Who pays for the excess food that stores throw away?
The customers pay for it, because its cost is hidden in the price of everything else.
What is Helen's advice?
She says we should compare the tiers, buy what we will really eat and not believe every myth.

lessons.title: Twelve Farms, One Truck
lessons.summary: Twelve farming families start a co-op, share one truck and bring water to their cherry trees.
lessons.text:
Twelve Farms, One Truck

Green Valley lies between two low hills, where the dirt roads turn soft every spring. For many years, the twelve families who farmed there sold their corn, hay and cherries on their own. Each family drove its own truck to the city, and each truck came back half empty. One evening in 2019, Sam Turner, who grew cherries on the east side of the valley, invited the other farmers to his kitchen. "We are all paying for the same road twelve times," he said. "Why don't we work together?"

That evening the families started a co-op. Every member paid 500 dollars to join, and with that money the co-op bought one large truck, one cold room and a small shop next to the main road. The shop sells exclusively what the members grow: sweet corn in summer, dark red cherries in June, honey, eggs and hay for people who keep horses. Because it sells exclusively local food, customers know where their dinner comes from.

The biggest problem was water. The cherry trees needed water in the dry months, but pumping it up from the river was expensive. Sam's neighbor, Rosa Diaz, had a better idea. A small lake lay near the top of the valley, so the co-op built a system of pipes that used gravity instead of electricity. The water simply ran down the hill. Each farm had a valve at the edge of its fields, and when a farmer opened the valve, gravity did the rest. Rosa checked every valve each morning in her tall rubber boots, walking through the wet dirt between the rows of corn and cherry trees.

The co-op also wanted its food to be certified as organic. To be certified, the farmers had to stop using toxic sprays for 3 years. Some members were worried, because without toxic sprays more of the corn was lost. However, certified food sold for a higher price, and the shop's customers were happy to pay it.

Today the co-op's truck leaves the valley every Tuesday and Friday, full of corn, cherries and hay. The members share the costs of fuel, repairs and the cold room, so each family pays far less than before. In the evenings they still meet in Sam's kitchen, with a row of dirty rubber boots by the door, to plan the next season.

Questions:
How did the families sell their food before the co-op?
Each family sold its corn, hay and cherries on its own and drove its own truck to the city.
What does the co-op's shop sell?
It sells exclusively what the members grow, such as corn, cherries, honey, eggs and hay.
How does the water reach the farms?
It runs down the hill from a small lake, because the pipes use gravity instead of electricity.
What does Rosa check every morning?
She checks every valve, walking through the wet dirt in her rubber boots.
What did the farmers have to do to be certified as organic?
They had to stop using toxic sprays for 3 years.
Why do the families pay less than before?
They share the costs of fuel, repairs and the cold room.

lessons.title: The House on the Cliff
lessons.summary: A couple rebuild an old officer's house on a cliff and run it as a bed and breakfast.
lessons.text:
The House on the Cliff

My husband, Tom, and I run a small bed and breakfast in Port Ellis, a fishing town on the northern coast. Our house stands at the edge of a cliff, about 50 meters above the sea. On calm mornings the water below the cliff is pearl gray, and the fishing boats at the old wooden dock look like toys. Later, in the sun, the sea shines like a pearl.

The house was formerly the home of a naval officer. Port Ellis was formerly a naval town, and in those days large gray ships lay at anchor in the bay. When the naval base closed in 1970, the town became quiet, and the officer's house was left to the wind. When we bought it 8 years ago, it was a wreck. The roof leaked, half the windows were broken, and birds lived in the kitchen.

We spent two years rebuilding it. We rebuilt the roof first, then the kitchen, then the 5 guest rooms. To pay for the work, we took a loan from the bank, and we did much of the rebuilding ourselves to keep the costs down. Rebuilding an old house teaches you to count every dollar.

Our prices change with the seasons. In summer, when the whales travel along the coast, every room is full, and we charge 160 dollars a night. Guests come from far away to watch the whales from the top of the cliff. In winter there are no whales and few guests, so a room costs only 90 dollars. The summer pays for the winter; that is the simple economics of our business.

Every morning I serve breakfast by the big window. Most guests drink coffee, but our English visitors often ask for Earl Grey, a black tea named after an English earl. The box shows a small drawing of the earl in a tall hat, and I keep 3 boxes in the kitchen, just in case.

After breakfast, many guests walk down a narrow path to the dock. A local man takes them out in his boat, and when they find a whale, he drops the anchor and turns off the engine so that everyone can listen to it breathe. An old iron anchor from the naval base now hangs in our front hall.

At night, when the last guest has gone to bed, I sometimes stand at the window and look at the lights of the boats in the bay. Eight years ago this house was a wreck. Today it pays for itself, and it is our home.

Questions:
Where does the bed and breakfast stand?
It stands at the edge of a cliff, about 50 meters above the sea.
Who formerly lived in the house?
A naval officer formerly lived there.
What was the house like when the couple bought it?
It was a wreck: the roof leaked, the windows were broken, and birds lived in the kitchen.
Why are prices higher in summer?
In summer the whales travel along the coast, and every room is full.
What is Earl Grey?
It is a black tea named after an English earl.
Why does the man drop the anchor?
He drops it so that the boat stays still and everyone can listen to the whale.

lessons.title: Forty Payments
lessons.summary: A house painter pays off the loan for his truck, one payment at a time, and plans what to do next.
lessons.text:
Forty Payments

Four years ago, James Cole, who paints houses for a living, needed a truck. His old one had broken down on a cold morning in January. A new truck was far too expensive, so James found a used one for 12,000 dollars and borrowed the money from his local bank. He had to pay it back in forty monthly payments of 340 dollars. When he signed the papers, forty payments sounded like forever.

He made a simple plan. Every Friday he put 85 dollars into a separate account, so that the money was ready when a payment was due. He also kept a small backup fund of 1,000 dollars in case work became slow. "Everyone needs a backup," his mother had told him when he was a boy, and he had never forgotten it.

The first year went well. The second year was harder. That winter James caught a nasty cold that lasted for weeks, and he could not work for most of February. Without the backup fund, he would have missed two payments. Instead he paid both on time, and subsequently he spent the spring rebuilding the fund, 50 dollars at a time.

On his kitchen wall, James kept a sheet of paper with forty boxes. Each time he paid, he drew a line through one box.

Last month James made the last of the forty payments. Then he awaited a letter from the bank confirming the completion of the loan. For a week he awaited it, checking the mail every afternoon. On a Tuesday the old phone in the kitchen rang, and he picked up the receiver. A friendly woman from the bank told him that the loan was paid and the truck now belonged to him. James held the receiver for a moment without speaking. Then he thanked her, put down the receiver and instantly felt lighter, as if he had put down a heavy bag.

The letter confirming the completion arrived subsequently, two days later. James pinned it next to the sheet with forty boxes.

That evening he sat with his wife, Ann, and talked about what he would do differently next time. "I would build a bigger backup fund before I borrowed," he said. "And I would compare banks. I didn't, and I should have." Ann smiled. "You did fine," she said. "We're blessed. You have work, a truck and no debt." James agreed that they were blessed. From now on, the 340 dollars would go into savings each month, and that money would instantly start working for them instead of for the bank.

Questions:
How many payments did James have to make?
He had to make forty monthly payments of 340 dollars.
Why did James keep a backup fund?
He kept it in case work became slow, because his mother had told him that everyone needs a backup.
Why could James not work in February?
He had a nasty cold that lasted for weeks.
How did James learn about the completion of the loan?
A woman from the bank phoned him, and the letter arrived subsequently.
How did James feel after he put down the receiver?
He instantly felt lighter, as if he had put down a heavy bag.
What would James do differently next time?
He would build a bigger backup fund first and compare banks.

lessons.title: Coins with a Face
lessons.summary: The shops on one old street start their own neighborhood money to keep spending close to home.
lessons.text:
Coins with a Face

Two years ago, the shop owners of Penn Street had a problem. A large shopping center had opened outside town, and fewer people walked down the old street. Nora Kim, who owned a small book store there, suggested an idea she had read about: a neighborhood currency. People would change their dollars into local money, which could be spent only in the shops on Penn Street. In this way, the money would stay in the neighborhood.

At first the idea was controversial. Some shop owners said customers would not understand it. Others feared it would mean extra work. Nora understood why it was controversial, but she believed it could spur people to shop close to home. At a meeting in her store, she explained that the local money would not replace the dollar. It would simply facilitate trade within the neighborhood, the way a common language makes conversation easier.

The group voted to try it for one year. They called the currency the Penn. One Penn was worth one dollar, and anyone who changed 20 dollars received 21 Penns, so there was a small incentive to use it. Only authorized shops could accept Penns, and each authorized shop put a green sign in its window. The local credit union agreed to be the only authorized place where people could change dollars into Penns and back again.

The money itself became a small work of art. The paper notes showed the old trees of Penn Street, and the 1 Penn coin was made of bronze. On the bronze coin was the face of Ruth Hale, a feminist and a pioneer, who opened the first shop on the street in 1912. As a feminist, she fought for the right of women to own a business. As a pioneer, she showed that it could be done.

On the first day, a long banner was hung across the street: "Spend it here, keep it here." The banner is still there today. Slowly the idea began to work. By the end of the year, Penns constituted about 1 dollar in every 10 spent on the street. That may sound small, but for a small shop it constituted real money. Furthermore, the project spurred something else: people began to talk to each other in the shops again.

The Penn is still a little controversial. However, on Saturday mornings, when Nora sees a child pay for a book with a bronze coin beneath the banner, she is sure it was worth trying.

Questions:
Why did fewer people walk down Penn Street?
A large shopping center had opened outside town.
Why was the idea controversial at first?
Some shop owners thought customers would not understand it, and others feared extra work.
How did Nora explain the purpose of the local money?
She said it would not replace the dollar but would facilitate trade within the neighborhood.
Where could people change dollars into Penns?
They could change them only at the local credit union, the only authorized place.
Whose face is on the bronze coin?
The face of Ruth Hale, a feminist and a pioneer who opened the first shop on the street, is on it.
What did the banner across the street say?
It said, "Spend it here, keep it here."

lessons.title: Old Records, New Buyers
lessons.summary: A young man sells his father's old records online and learns how buyers find a small seller.
lessons.text:
Old Records, New Buyers

For 30 years, Ben Ortiz's father ran a small record shop in the center of town. When he retired, the shop closed, and about 4,000 records and discs moved into the family garage. Ben, who was 24 and looking for work, decided to try something new. He would become an online seller.

He spent the first month sorting. Each record went into a box by type: folk, punk, rap, gospel, jazz and rock. His father had especially loved gospel, and there were whole boxes of gospel records from small church groups, made long before Ben was born. There were also boxes of early rap, folk songs with simple guitar covers, and loud punk records with angry drawings on the front. Ben checked every disc for damage, cleaned it carefully and wrote down its condition.

At first, nobody found him. He listed 200 records on a large music website, and in two weeks he sold only one. A friend who worked with computers explained the problem. The website used an algorithm to decide which sellers appeared first, and the algorithm favored sellers with many good reviews and clear photos. A new seller with no reviews was almost impossible to find.

So Ben changed his methods. He took bright, sharp photos of every cover in the light of the garage window. He wrote honest descriptions, mentioning even a small mark on a disc. He packed each order with care and sent it the next morning. Slowly the reviews came. Most of them were anonymous, signed only with a first letter or a made-up name, but they were kind. One anonymous buyer wrote: "Better than described, and fast." Another anonymous buyer simply wrote: "A real music lover." With every good review, the algorithm showed his records to more people.

Then a well-known music blog wrote about a rare punk record that Ben had found in a corner of the garage. Suddenly there was a buzz around his little shop. For three days his phone buzzed every few minutes with a new order. Buyers asked about folk records from the same year, and a church in Ohio bought 40 of his father's gospel records for its library.

Today Ben earns a small but steady income. His father sometimes visits the garage, picks up a disc and tells the story of the day he bought it. Ben has learned that a small seller cannot fight an algorithm, but he can earn its trust, one honest description at a time.

Questions:
Where did the records go when the shop closed?
About 4,000 records and discs moved into the family garage.
What types of music did Ben find?
He found folk, punk, rap, gospel, jazz and rock.
Why did nobody find Ben's records at first?
The website's algorithm favored sellers with many good reviews, and he had none.
What did Ben change?
He took clear photos, wrote honest descriptions and sent each order the next morning.
What were most of the reviews like?
Most of them were anonymous, but they were kind.
What created a buzz around Ben's shop?
A music blog wrote about a rare punk record that he had found.

lessons.title: Sauce at the Saturday Market
lessons.summary: A woman sells her own pepper sauce at a farmers' market and gives a cooking demonstration.
lessons.text:
Sauce at the Saturday Market

Every Saturday from May to October, Grace Lin sets up her table at the farmers' market in the old town square. Beneath a red and white roof, she places rows of small glass bottles filled with her own pepper sauce. The sauce is a blend of red peppers, honey, a little salt and a few secret spices. Grace has worked on the blend for 6 years, and she will not tell anyone the exact amounts.

Her sauce costs 8 dollars a bottle, which is more than a bottle from a big store. Grace knows this, so she has two simple rules. First, she never uses anything artificial: no artificial colors, no artificial flavors. Second, she lets people taste before they buy. She believes that a good product is its own best advertising.

People often stop to admire her table. They admire the bright bottles, which shine in the morning sun like small red lights. But admiring is not buying, and Grace learned early that a sale needs something more. So, three years ago, she began to give a cooking demonstration every Saturday at 11 in the morning.

The demonstration is always simple. Grace heats a pan over a small gas flame, cooks some vegetables from the next table, and adds a little sauce at the end. Then she tosses everything together and hands out small paper cups to the crowd. "You don't need much," she tells them. "A good sauce should enhance the vegetables, not hide them." She tosses a second pan of rice and sauce, and the smell travels across the square. After each demonstration, she usually sells 20 bottles in half an hour.

The honey seller at the next table, an old friend named Mark, likes to say that he is jealous. "Your crowd is bigger than mine," he says with a smile. He is not really jealous, though, because Grace buys all her honey from him. Her success helps his business too, and they both know it.

At the last market in October, the square fills with children in costumes. One year a little girl dressed as a witch, in a tall black hat, came back to the demonstration three times. The third time, her mother laughed and bought two bottles. "My little witch has made her decision," she said.

When the market closes, Grace packs the empty boxes beneath her table and counts the day's money. Then she walks home, already thinking about how to enhance next week's demonstration.

Questions:
What is Grace's sauce made of?
It is a blend of red peppers, honey, a little salt and a few secret spices.
What are Grace's two rules?
She never uses anything artificial, and she lets people taste before they buy.
Why did Grace start the demonstration?
She learned that people admired her table but did not always buy, so a sale needed something more.
What does Grace say about using the sauce?
She says a good sauce should enhance the vegetables, not hide them.
Why is Mark not really jealous?
He is not really jealous because Grace buys all her honey from him.
What did the little witch do at the last market?
She came back to the demonstration three times, and her mother bought two bottles.

lessons.title: The Fix-It Club
lessons.summary: On the first Saturday of every month, neighbors bring broken things to a hall and fix them together.
lessons.text:
The Fix-It Club

On the first Saturday of every month, the community hall on River Road becomes the Fix-It Club. From ten until two, people bring in their broken things, and a group of patient volunteers helps them with the repairs. There is coffee, and there is no charge. The only rule is that you stay and watch, so that next time you can do the repair yourself.

The club was started by Frank Weber, a retired engineer with large, careful hands. For 40 years he repaired machines in a factory, and he never got used to the idea that people throw away a radio because of one loose wire. "Most things are not really broken," he says. "They are simply waiting for a new bolt and a little care."

On a typical Saturday, the tables fill quickly. A young father brings a child's chair with a missing bolt. An old woman brings a winter jacket that no longer closes, and a story about her late husband, who wore it for 30 years. Frank finds the right bolt for the chair in one of his many small boxes and shows the father how to fit it. Ten minutes later the chair is fully functional again.

Not every repair is a pleasure. Last month a man brought in a coffee machine that had not been cleaned for years. When Frank opened it, the inside was truly disgusting: brown, wet and smelling of old milk. Everyone laughed at the disgusting sight, and then they cleaned it together. The machine worked perfectly. It had never been broken; it had only been dirty.

Some things cannot be saved. Modern phones and ultra-thin computers are often closed with special screws, and some ultra-cheap products are made so that nobody can open them at all.

The club also helps people think about their usage of energy and water. Volunteers check old machines, and they show how small changes can lower usage at home. They actively look for new volunteers, especially young people who want to learn, and Frank actively teaches every new volunteer himself.

"When we throw something away, someone is always the loser," Frank says. "Usually it is our bank account. Sometimes it is the planet." At the Fix-It Club, he hopes, nobody has to be the loser. A functional chair and a clean coffee machine are small things, but they add up.

Questions:
What happens at the Fix-It Club?
Volunteers help people repair their broken things, and people stay and watch so that they can learn.
Who started the club?
Frank Weber, a retired engineer, started it.
What did Frank do for the child's chair?
He found the right bolt and showed the father how to fit it, so the chair was functional again.
Why was the coffee machine disgusting?
It had not been cleaned for years, and the inside was brown, wet and smelled of old milk.
Why are some products hard to repair?
Some ultra-thin computers use special screws, and some ultra-cheap products cannot be opened at all.
Who is the loser when we throw something away, according to Frank?
Usually our bank account is the loser, and sometimes the planet is.

lessons.title: Choosing a Profession
lessons.summary: A newspaper adviser answers a young reader who must choose between three professions.
lessons.text:
Choosing a Profession

Dear Ms. Grant,

I am 18 and will finish school this summer. I cannot decide which profession to choose. I am thinking about three: nursing, working as a personal trainer, or becoming a cook like my uncle. My parents say I should choose the one that pays best. My friends say I should follow my heart. Online there is so much commentary about which jobs will disappear that the more commentary I read, the more confused I feel. What should I do?

Owen

Dear Owen,

Choosing a profession is one of the biggest economic decisions of your life. Let me suggest a simple tool.

Take a large sheet of paper and draw a matrix: a table with rows and columns. Write your three choices down the side. Across the top, write what matters to you: the cost of training, the years of study, the expected income, the hours, and how much you would enjoy the work. Then fill in every box of the matrix honestly. The matrix will not make the decision for you, but it will show you each choice clearly.

Each profession has its merits. Nursing is a healing profession, and many people find deep meaning in healing others. Nurses are needed everywhere, so the work is steady. However, the training takes several years, and the hours can be long. A personal trainer can start working quickly, after a short course, and a good trainer can build a steady group of clients. On the other hand, a trainer's income is often less certain, especially at the beginning. A cook can learn in a kitchen while being paid, but the pay is low at first, and the work happens in the evenings and on weekends.

Ask yourself what kind of person you are. Are you oriented toward people, or toward practical work with your hands? A nurse and a trainer are strongly oriented toward people. A cook spends more time with pans than with conversations. Neither is better; they are simply different.

As for the commentary about the future, remember one thing. Every profession will change, so adaptation is part of every career. The workers who do well are not the ones who choose a perfect job, but the ones who are ready for adaptation. Healing, cooking and teaching will always be needed, even if the tools change.

Finally, talk to real people. Ask your uncle, a nurse and a trainer about their days. Then return to your matrix and look at it again.

With best wishes,
Diane Grant

Questions:
Which three professions is Owen thinking about?
He is thinking about nursing, working as a personal trainer, and becoming a cook.
Why does Owen feel confused?
He feels confused because he has read so much commentary about which jobs will disappear.
What is the matrix that Ms. Grant suggests?
It is a table with Owen's three choices down the side and what matters to him across the top.
What are the merits of nursing?
It is a healing profession with deep meaning, and the work is steady.
Which professions are oriented toward people?
Nursing and the work of a personal trainer are oriented toward people.
Why is adaptation part of every career?
It is part of every career because every profession will change.

lessons.title: The Rialto Cinema
lessons.summary: A family keeps a small old cinema open with help from local businesses and a student film premiere.
lessons.text:
The Rialto Cinema

The Rialto Cinema has stood on the corner of Bridge Street since 1938. When it opened, the town caught a kind of cinema fever. People dressed in their best clothes, stood in long lines in the rain, and talked about the films for days. The fever lasted for many years. Today the Rialto is one of the last small cinemas in the area, with a single screen, 200 red seats and a ceiling painted with gold stars.

Peter Shaw and his daughter, Julia, run the cinema together. For the Shaw family, Friday nights are sacred. Whatever happens, the Rialto shows a film on Friday night, and Peter stands at the door to greet each guest by name. Julia sells the tickets and the famous chocolate cake, which Peter's mother first made 60 years ago. Locals say the cake is legendary, and some of them come as much for the legendary cake as for the films.

Running a small cinema is not easy. A ticket costs 9 dollars, and after paying for the films, the electricity and the staff, the family keeps only a little. Because of the popularity of streaming, fewer people go out to the cinema. Peter understands the popularity of streaming; he watches films at home too. Still, he believes that laughing with 200 strangers in the dark is something a living room cannot give.

Last spring the family received an unexpected bill. The old heating system had to be replaced, and the cost was 30,000 dollars. The bill was unexpected, but Julia had a plan. She asked local businesses to help. The bread shop, the book store and the paint store each sponsored one month of films, and their names appeared on the screen before every show. The businesses that sponsored the Rialto were pleased, because hundreds of people saw their names each week.

Julia had a second idea. Students at the local college had made a short animation about the history of the town. It was full of bright colors and soft music, and the students had worked on the animation for a year. Julia offered to hold its premiere at the Rialto. On the night of the premiere, every seat was full. The students stood at the front, and when the film ended, the whole room stood up and cheered. The money from the premiere paid for a large part of the new heating.

Since then, the Rialto's popularity has grown. On Friday nights there are lines on Bridge Street again, not quite like in 1938, but close.

Questions:
What happened in the town when the cinema opened?
The town caught a kind of cinema fever.
Why are Friday nights sacred to the Shaw family?
They are sacred because the Rialto shows a film on Friday night, whatever happens.
Why is the chocolate cake legendary?
Peter's mother first made it 60 years ago, and some people come as much for the cake as for the films.
What unexpected bill did the family receive?
They had to replace the old heating system, which cost 30,000 dollars.
How did local businesses help?
They each sponsored one month of films, and their names appeared on the screen.
What happened at the premiere of the students' animation?
Every seat was full, and the whole room stood up and cheered at the end.
